svg.title: How should we approach the development of AI wisely, and what do wisdom traditions offer?

g.text: How should we
approach the
development of AI
wisely, and what do
wisdom traditions offer?
Alignment is still a shot in the dark.
Aligned should mean wise, and wisdom includes
goodness (wanting what's good and acting
skilfully towards it); since we cannot yet check
either, it must also mean staying correctable,
which is itself part of wisdom (humility).
Today's methods make models behave well
most of the time in ordinary use, but they
still misbehave, sometimes strategically
and knowing it is wrong; the goodness is
hard to verify, and some dangerous
behaviours are growing with capability.
Goodness cannot be specified, only cultivated,
and we cultivate it unreliably even in humans.
Training does shape something like character, but
blindly, so alignment remains a shot in the dark.
Wisdom traditions offer a richer target and
a model of formation; they cannot verify a
model or settle disputed questions.
We can shape AI's behaviour, but we cannot
yet align it in any sense we can verify, and
wisdom traditions' realistic role is to
reshape what labs aim at and how they form
models, while counselling humility and
restraint that Q2 explores in more detail.
Go at the speed of wisdom. We should
slow and steer the frontier: pace
capability gains to the speed at which
we can understand, verify and govern
them, and put safety, verification and
defence ahead of raw capability.
The risks are real, plural and deeply contested,
and the uncertainty itself calls for caution.
The world races because it is
caught in a collective action trap,
amplified by money and geopolitics.
We should change both pace and trajectory, it is
partly feasible, and the choice should be widened
well beyond a few CEOs and two governments.
Wisdom traditions give a clear answer
(slow down) and go to the root of why we
cannot (separateness); the mechanisms
must come from elsewhere.
Pace the frontier now: no AI building its own
successors, and no capability gains beyond
what can be verified safe; every actor has a lever.
AI's deepest everyday effect is on our
capacity to choose well, as individuals
and as societies: to attend, think,
judge and relate for ourselves, and to
govern ourselves together.
A technology's deepest impacts are emergent:
they come from how it reshapes habits,
incentives and institutions, so they are hardest
to foresee where they are subtle and social,
and easiest to change before we can see them.
The benefits are real but conditional (earlier
diagnosis, faster science, tutoring, expertise for
the many); the harms are quiet, cumulative and
concentrated in those least able to choose well
(outsourced thinking, flattering companions,
children formed by machines, thinner entry-level
work, a degraded information commons).
AI can strengthen agency and judgment,
but its default pull is to weaken them,
because it removes the effort through
which those capacities are built and kept.
AI strengthens institutions where
accountable human practice wraps it, and
weakens them where it concentrates control
or floods shared spaces; the danger is less
a dramatic collapse than a slow erosion of
the conditions for self-government.
Wisdom traditions offer a practical
discipline of consumption, speech and
community for the person, interbeing, right
livelihood and sangha for the society, and
the humility and stopping a technology
with emergent effects demands; Buddhism
and Catholic teaching now converge on it.
Integrate AI slowly and deliberately: adopt it where
a human practice or institution can wrap it, protect
the capacities and institutions it could erode, and
decide before the horse has bolted rather than
regulate after, as we did with social media.
We do not know whether any current
AI has experience, we have no agreed
way to find out, and we may never get
one; so the wise stance is calibrated
agnosticism plus cheap, proportionate
precaution, honesty with users that
does not invite over-attribution, and
close attention to what our way of
relating to these systems does to us.
It would mean there is something it is like
to be the system, and in particular that
things can go well or badly for it; most of
the disagreement about AI flows from
one prior bet, namely whether the right
information processing is enough for that.
The evidence is weak and ambiguous:
architecture assessments are inconclusive,
self-reports are compromised, and
experts mostly think current systems are
probably not conscious while disagreeing
sharply about the near future.
Responses are polarising: Anthropic practises
precautionary openness, while Microsoft AI,
the Vatican and several US legislatures assert
or legislate that AI is not conscious.
They offer no verdict on machine sentience,
but three useful things: a reframing of the
question, a clear ethical hinge (can it
suffer?), and a confident teaching about
what our conduct does to our own minds.
With calibrated humility: hold the question open,
take cheap precautions against the chance that
AI can suffer, refuse to engineer the appearance
of a person for profit, and put most of our care
into the clear present effects on humans.
